 4         19. Microsoft Corporation and Mojang AB own, operate, and control the
 5   “Minecraft” family of websites, applications, and online services, including but not

10   Education Edition.”
11         20. When California users—including minor children—visit the Minecraft
12   Properties or use Minecraft-related services, their devices engage in continuous
13   electronic communications with Defendants’ servers. These communications
14   include HTTP/HTTPS requests and responses, page and form content, search
15   queries, clicks and scrolls, video interactions, and other data necessary to render
16   pages, authenticate users, and deliver content.
17         21. In addition to what is technically necessary to provide the requested
18   service, Defendants have implemented a covert tracking and surveillance
19   architecture on the Minecraft Properties. This tracking stack includes, among other
20   tools, Microsoft’s own “Clarity” session-replay code, Adobe “Helix RUM” (Real
21   User Monitoring), Microsoft “OneCollector” telemetry endpoints, “Microsoft
22   Target” personalization endpoints, and other analytics and performance scripts that
23   silently log users’ behavior and device characteristics.
24         22. When a user—adult or child—loads a Minecraft Property in a browser or
25   app, Defendants’ code automatically fetches and executes these tracking scripts.
26   This occurs immediately upon page load, often before any cookie banner or privacy
27   notice is rendered, and regardless of whether the user has created an account, logged
28   in, or affirmatively agreed to any terms.
                                                 8

 1         23. The session-replay components, including Microsoft Clarity, capture and
 2   reconstruct users’ interactions on Minecraft web pages essentially “click-by-click.”
 3   These tools record mouse movements, clicks, scrolls, keystrokes, typed text, focus
 4   changes, and other granular interaction signals, then transmit that data in real time
 5   to Microsoft-controlled servers for analysis. From Defendants’ vantage point, this
 6   provides a near-complete replay of what the user saw and did on the page, as though
 7   Defendants were looking over the user’s shoulder the entire time.
 8         24. Defendants’ tracking stack also performs device fingerprinting. Scripts on
 9   the Minecraft Properties quietly execute functions such as canvas operations (e.g.,
10   calls to canvas.getContext()), audio and hardware profiling, and inspection of
11   browser properties like navigator.deviceMemory and hardwareConcurrency to
12   generate unique, persistent signatures of each user’s device. These fingerprints
13   enable Defendants to recognize and track a device across sessions—even if cookies
14   are deleted or the user attempts to use “private” or “incognito” browsing modes.
15         25. In addition, the Minecraft Properties send frequent telemetry beacons to
16   Microsoft’s    data-collection    endpoints,   including   but    not   limited    to
17   browser.events.data.microsoft.com and target.microsoft.com. These telemetry calls
18   include unique identifiers (such as Microsoft cookies and session IDs), device
19   fingerprints, browser and device configuration data, timestamps, navigation paths,
20   and detailed usage metrics reflecting exactly how a user moved through the site or
21   application.
22         26. Defendants further embed and integrate tracking with third-party services
23   such as Adobe analytics/real-user monitoring, Akamai mPulse, and embedded video
24   players (including YouTube or similar platforms). As a result, when users interact
25   with embedded media or even simply view pages containing these elements,
26   additional domains controlled by those third parties receive data about the user’s
27   communications, viewing behavior, and device characteristics—again without clear
28   disclosure or informed consent.
                                               9
                              CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT

 1         27. These tracking behaviors occur not only on the main consumer-facing
 2   Minecraft website but also on child-directed and education-facing properties. For

10   contents of users’ electronic communications with the Minecraft Properties in real
11   time, including: the specific URLs and pages visited; search queries or text entered
12   into forms; the sequence and timing of clicks, scrolls, and interactions; and in some
13   instances, details about which videos were viewed and how users engaged with those
14   videos. These are more than mere “headers” or routing information; they reflect the
15   substance of what users are viewing, requesting, and doing online.
16         29. Defendants link this behavioral and content data to persistent identifiers
17   and device fingerprints, allowing them to build detailed profiles of individual users
18   and devices across sessions and contexts. Over time, Defendants can associate
19   multiple visits and interactions with the same person or household, even where the
20   user attempts to limit tracking by clearing cookies, using different browsers, or
21   switching between home and school devices.
22         30. Neither Plaintiffs nor reasonable Minecraft users were informed—in a
23   clear, conspicuous, and timely manner—that the Minecraft Properties are wired with
24   session-replay, fingerprinting, and telemetry tools that operate in this way.
25   Defendants’ public-facing privacy disclosures use vague, generic references to
26   “analytics,” “cookies,” or “personalization,” and do not adequately explain that
27   every movement and keystroke on the site may be recorded and stored, or that
28   persistent device fingerprints will track users across visits.

 1         31. Any purported consent Defendants rely on is invalid for multiple reasons.
 2   To the extent cookie banners or pop-ups appear at all, they are typically displayed

 9   their children’s communications.
10         32. Defendants’ conduct is particularly egregious in child-focused and
11   education contexts. When minors in California access Minecraft: Education Edition
12   or related learning resources, they and their parents reasonably expect that their
13   activity will be used for instructional or limited operational purposes, not to fuel a
14   hidden web of analytics, profiling, and cross-site tracking. Nonetheless, Defendants
15   collect and transmit persistent identifiers and detailed behavioral telemetry from
16   these child users without verifiable parental consent and for purposes that go far
17   beyond narrow “internal operations.”
18         33. Defendants did not implement this surveillance infrastructure for purely
19   benign or narrow security purposes. The detailed data they harvest—from session
20   replays, fingerprints, telemetry, and embedded third-party integrations—is a critical
21   commercial asset that supports their broader business goals, including product
22   optimization, personalization, and marketing. By closely monitoring how users
23   (including children) interact with Minecraft content, Defendants can test and refine
24   designs, adjust promotions, encourage longer engagement, and better target features,
25   offerings, and advertising.
26         34. In the modern digital economy, this type of granular behavioral and device
27   data is highly valuable. Large technology companies, including Defendants,
28   routinely leverage user data as a key input into analytics, recommendation engines,
                                              11

             Case 3:25-cv-11078-SK      Document 1     Filed 01/02/26   Page 12 of 53




 1   and advertising systems that drive revenue and competitive advantage. The more
 2   detailed and persistent the tracking, the more useful it becomes for modeling user

 4         35. By surreptitiously collecting, retaining, and exploiting Plaintiffs’ and
 5   Class members’ data in this manner, Defendants deprived them of the ability to
 6   control how their personal information and online activities are used and to decide

10         36. Plaintiffs and Class members suffered privacy harms as a result of
11   Defendants’ conduct, including the loss of control over confidential communications
12   and personal information, the invasion of their seclusion, the exposure of their online

14   commercial benefit. For children and families using Minecraft in educational or
15   child-directed contexts, these intrusions are especially offensive and contrary to
16   reasonable expectations of privacy.

19   with respect to the Minecraft Properties. The identities and precise roles of additional
